---
title: "Using Claude Code inside VS Code"
subtitle: "The friendlier entry point if you'd rather not work in a bare terminal."
---

If you've spent your career in graphical environments — RStudio, Stata's
window, Matlab's IDE — running Claude Code in a bare terminal can feel
awkward. **Visual Studio Code ("VS Code") is the gentlest landing pad.**
It is free and graphical, has a built-in terminal, shows proposed code
edits in a normal side-by-side diff view, and knows about Git. I'd start
here, and drop back to the bare terminal only if it starts getting in the
way.

::: {.callout-tip}
You'll still want to skim the [terminal primer](terminal-and-bash.qmd) so
you can read what Claude Code is doing in the terminal pane at the bottom
of VS Code. But you don't need to be comfortable with the terminal; you
just need to be able to read it.
:::

## Why this is the easier starting point

| In a bare terminal | In VS Code |
|---|---|
| Code edits show up as a wall of text diffs | Edits appear in a familiar side-by-side diff pane |
| File paths in Claude's output are just strings | File paths are clickable; Cmd-click jumps you to line and column |
| You alt-tab between Stata/RStudio and the terminal | The integrated terminal sits at the bottom of the same window |
| Recovering from a bad edit means `git checkout` | Cmd-Z works in the file you're looking at, just like always |
| Git status is a separate command | The Source Control pane shows changes file-by-file in real time |

None of these are revolutionary. Together they remove enough small friction
that "I'll try Claude Code today" stops feeling like a project of its own.

## Step 1 — Install VS Code

Download from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com).
The installer is signed and behaves like any other Mac app — drag to
Applications, open, accept the security prompt the first time.

If you already have VS Code, skip this step.

## Step 2 — Install the Claude Code extension

VS Code has an extension marketplace. The official **Claude Code**
extension by Anthropic gives you in-editor integration with the
CLI you installed earlier. It is optional — you can use Claude Code in
VS Code's integrated terminal without it — but it is a small install
that pays for itself the first time you accept a diff inside the editor
instead of squinting at one in the terminal.

To install:

1. Click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (or press
   `Cmd+Shift+X`).
2. Search for `Claude Code`.
3. Install the one published by **Anthropic**.

What the extension adds (paraphrased — see the extension's own page for
the canonical list):

- **Native diff view.** When Claude proposes an edit, the change opens
  in VS Code's diff editor instead of being printed to the terminal. You
  approve or reject with a button.
- **Open-file and selection awareness.** Claude can see which file you
  have focused and what you have selected, so "rewrite the highlighted
  paragraph" works without you naming the file.
- **Tighter back-and-forth** when you're switching between editing a
  file by hand and asking Claude to take over.

If you skip the extension, everything still works — just through the
integrated terminal. The next steps are the same either way.

## Step 3 — Open your project folder

`File → Open Folder…` and pick the project you want Claude to work on
(a paper draft, a teaching repo, a replication package — whatever you'd
like to start with).

The left sidebar now shows the file tree of that folder. This is the
mental anchor: **the folder you opened is the folder Claude Code will
have access to**, nothing more.

## Step 4 — Open the integrated terminal

Press `Ctrl+`` (the backtick key, top-left on most keyboards). A terminal
pane appears at the bottom of the VS Code window.

This is the same terminal from the [terminal primer](terminal-and-bash.qmd)
— it just lives inside VS Code now. Two things to notice:

- It already starts in the folder you opened. No `cd` needed.
- You can drag its top edge up and down to give it more or less space.

## Step 5 — Start Claude Code

In the integrated terminal, type:

```bash
claude
```

…and hit Return. The first time, you'll be prompted to log in (a browser
tab will open) and to choose a few preferences. Accept the defaults.

You're now at Claude Code's prompt, **inside the VS Code window of your
project**. Type a question or instruction the same way you would in a
bare terminal. The difference is what happens next: when Claude proposes
to edit a file, the diff appears in the editor pane above, not in the
terminal below. Click *Accept*, *Reject*, or open the file to edit
yourself.

## A first session in VS Code, end to end

Try this with any project of yours:

1. `File → Open Folder…` and pick a small project.
2. `Ctrl+`` to open the terminal; type `claude`; Return.
3. At the prompt: *"Read the project. In one paragraph, what does it do?"*
4. Watch the editor: as Claude reads files, you'll see it open them in
   the editor pane (with the extension) or just see the `Read` tool
   calls in the terminal (without).
5. Now: *"Add a one-line comment at the top of every `.do` file naming
   the script. Show me each diff before applying."*
6. Each proposed edit opens in a diff view. Click through, approve or
   reject, watch the file tree's Git indicators (M for modified) light
   up in the sidebar.
7. Open the Source Control pane (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) — every change Claude
   has accepted is right there, with line-by-line diffs, ready to
   commit if you want.

The first time you run this loop, the difference from "chat in a browser"
is obvious: your attention goes to deciding what to ask, not to shuttling
text back and forth.

## Language extensions worth installing

VS Code is a general editor. The extensions below add the language
support most economists need. All are free and well-maintained.

| You write… | Install |
|---|---|
| **R** | "R" by REditorSupport, plus "R Debugger" |
| **Python** | "Python" by Microsoft (covers pylance, debugger, formatter) |
| **Julia** | "Julia" by julialang |
| **Stata** | "Stata Enhanced" by Kyle Barron — syntax highlighting + run-in-Stata |
| **Matlab** | "MATLAB" by MathWorks |
| **LaTeX** | "LaTeX Workshop" by James Yu — compile + preview + jump-to-source |
| **Quarto** | "Quarto" by quarto.dev — render + preview .qmd files |

Optional but pleasant:

- **GitLens** — adds blame, history, and rich Git information in the
  gutter and hover tooltips.
- **Even Better TOML** / **YAML** — for configuration files (Quarto,
  Julia projects).
- **vscode-icons** or **Material Icon Theme** — file-tree icons that
  make `.do`, `.dta`, `.tex`, `.R`, `.py` visually distinct.

::: {.callout-note}
None of these extensions are required for Claude Code. They make *you*
more productive in the editor when Claude isn't doing the work.
:::

## Keyboard shortcuts that matter

If you remember three: `Ctrl+`` (terminal), `Cmd+P` (jump to file),
`Cmd+Shift+P` (run any command).

| Shortcut (Mac) | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+`` | Toggle the integrated terminal |
| `Ctrl+Shift+`` | Open a *new* terminal (you can have several) |
| `Cmd+P` | Jump to a file by typing part of its name |
| `Cmd+Shift+P` | Command palette — run any VS Code command |
| `Cmd+B` | Toggle the file-tree sidebar |
| `Cmd+\` | Split the editor into two panes side by side |
| `Cmd+S` | Save the current file |
| `Cmd+Z` / `Cmd+Shift+Z` | Undo / redo, file by file |

(On Windows/Linux, swap `Cmd` for `Ctrl` and the shortcuts above
work the same way.)

## When to drop back to the bare terminal

VS Code is the easier path; it is not the only path. Reasons to use the
bare Terminal app instead:

- You want a **full-screen Claude Code session** with no editor
  distractions — reviewing a long replication audit, say.
- You're **SSHed into a server** (a research computing cluster, for
  example) and don't have VS Code there.
- VS Code isn't installed on the machine you're sitting at.
- You're already in a Terminal session for other reasons (running a
  long Stata batch job, watching a build).

The two are interchangeable. Anything you do in one works in the other.
